# Re-Running 2024

The 2024 data showed promise, but it had two major problems: 1) the
initialization energies were random (the desired temperature is an
input, but this only set the variance of each velocity distribution;
since the temperature would be the variance of the generated velocities,
it was random too), and 2) the potential energy had a step at `rskn`,
the range of the force. While this wouldn't affect the calculation in
any way, it creates noise in the total energy, which would experience
steps as particles moved in and out of interaction range.

Finally, the last version (V1.2) of the *Julia* code did not have the
ability to heat or cool, nor did it have the ability to estimate
dispersion. This set of experiments will re-run the important part of
the 2024 runs, restricting the upper energy range (there were useless
higher energy runs) and adding more runs in the transition neighborhood.
The program still uses a temperature number as an integer to set the
initialization temperature. This number is divided by 1,000 set the
temperature of the particles at $t=0$. Previously we had executed 100
different temperatures running from 1 to 100.

## Preparing for the Runs

We'll read in a the last version of the data file and rename it.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DF.C
MD2DF.C <- readRDS("../MD2DF.C.RDS")
setkey( MD2DF.C, "TE.mean.rs")
```

The transition region was narrowed to total energies of 0.1535 and
0.1576. @fig-Final2 shows the data at the end of the last set of runs.

![Close‑up of the transition region as identified in `Final2.pdf`,
clearly showing where adding energy does not change the temperature.
Thick black lines are weighted regressions of the solid region (valid
points below 0.1535), and the fluid region (all points above 0.157), and
the red line is the transition region drawn between (intersecting) the
two regression lines. 1$\sigma$ confidence intervals of measurements are
plotted as light blue region along with the regression lines, as well as
gray region showing the maximum ‑ minimum range for each measurement.
Points are shown as black circles and red triangles (valid and not valid
points, respectively). 95% confidence intervals on the regression
predictions are shown in thin blue lines.](../tregz4.png){#fig-Final2}

The full data collection goes from a TE of 0.1284 to 0.23135, and these
are high by on average about 0.01167 due to the PE step. @fig-keTE.C is
a plot of the temperature vs total energy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-keTE.C
#| fig-cap: Full data plot, with the gray band showing the standard deviation of the temperature estimates (not adjusted for the number of samples in the avereage). Red triangles are not considered valid averages.
plotconfMD2( y="ke", df = MD2DF.C[ TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.0, 0.4),],
              linethresh = 200, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle",
              ylab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle") # sets up plot
grid( col = "darkgray")
```

We don't need so many high energy points, so we should start spacing
them out at the higher energies. @tbl-MD2DF.Ch shows the points
approaching a total energy of 0.175:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-MD2DF.Ch
#| tbl-cap: Points approaching total energy of 0.175.
# output: asis
knitr::kable( MD2DF.C[TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.168, 0.175),
        .(TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, energy, valid)])
```

We can use the above to see that initialization energies up to 42 or so
will cover the range of interest. Above that we can space them by two
and then three to get get a few high energy samples

The transition region itself only had seven samples within the region
(@tbl-MD2DF.Ctr).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-MD2DF.Ctr
#| tbl-cap: Initialization and mean total energies near the transition region, with kinetic energy (i.e. temperature), run id, and valid flag. 
trnrgn <- MD2DF.C[TE.mean.rs %within%  c(0.1534, 0.1576),
         .(TE.init, TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, run, valid)]
knitr::kable( trnrgn)
```

The `S2b` series did have temperature correction at initialization, so
let's look at the progression of the energies (@fig-S2binitstep).

```{r}
#| label: fig-S2binitstep
#| fig-cap: Total Energy steps.  Each point is the energy delta from the previous energy initialization to the plotted one. Thus, the delta plotted at 30 is the energy change from 29 to 30.
S2b <- MD2DF.C[series == "S2b",
         .(TE.init, TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, series, energy, valid)]
dtrn <- diff(S2b$TE.mean.rs)
mean( dtrn)
plot( x= tail( as.numeric( S2b$energy),-1), y = dtrn, 
      xlab = "Init Temp", ylab = "Delta TE", 
      main = "Series S2b Initialization", panel.first = grid())
```

The mean step is almost the 0.001 that the code implemented.
Unfortunately, the PE step gives a variance to the total energy that
depends on the particle trajectories. We can expected that variance to
be reduced by the elimination of the step.

## New Series

The new series will examine 50 temperature steps from 1 - 50 (the input
is an integer temperature which is divided by 1,000), eleven steps of
two from 52 to 72, and nine steps of three from 75 to 99. We'll probably
run a 100 too, for a total of 71 runs. Well run all the energies to 10k
steps and then we will look to see which energies now appear to be in
the transition region. These will will run to 4M steps, and then start
diffusion calculations (first executed on 6 April 2025, but an error was
found, so it was re-executed on 9 April).

## First Tranche

``` julia
julia> td = "/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/Data/1980"
julia> tlist = vcat([i for i in 1:50], [i for i in 52:2:72], 
                    [i for i in 75:3:100], [100])
julia> @time MD2.newruns( td, tlist, "S3.", 1000, 5000, 6)
 77.023278 seconds (132.86 M allocations: 10.292 GiB, 3.43% gc time, 88 lock 
 conflicts, 2.40% compilation time)
```

The data is in the following directory:

```{r}
#| label: datadir
datadir = "/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/Data/1980"
```

That was 71 energies of 31k steps each, for a total of 2,201k steps in
77s, or 0.034s/1k steps. The code above was slightly modified from what
was actually run: a "dot" (".") was put in the "S3." input above. This
was forgotten in the original run, and that input was copied, so the
files were created without a dot between the series and the energy. This
was corrected with the unix command `rename "s/S3(.*)/S3.$1/" S3*`.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DF.D
MD2DF.D <- MD2DFfile( "../MD2DF.D.RDS", datadir, "S3.*.csv", df = MD2DF.C)
```

The data is plotted in @fig-MD2DF.D, with the temperature vs. total
energy in @fig-keTE.D below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.D
#| fig-cap: "All (or most) of the (now) 60 columns represented one way or another below. The first eight plots are simply `plotScalars` (that is, `ke sd`, `ke`, Pressure, relative temperature variamce `rtv`, $r^2$ of temperature regression, ke relative range, $<\\psi>$, all plotted againt total energy, and  . These are followed by (left to right, top to bottom) `TE Range` (`TE.max.raw - TE.min.raw` in open symbols, and `TE.sd.rs` in closed symbols, plotted logrithmically), Momentum squared (with standard deviation and range), Maximum of momentum squared vs. total steps, spectral width (in units of $1 / \\tau$), $ \\psi$ delta -  the difference berween `psiabs` and `psiavg`, and at the bottem left total steps."
op <- par( mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 0.5, 0.5), tcl = -0.3,
mgp = c(1.7, 0.4, 0))
plotAllMD2(MD2DF.D[series == "S3"], linethresh = 200)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-keTE.D
#| fig-cap: "Temperature (i.e., mean kinetic energy) for series 3.  Red triangles are measurements not considered valid."
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.D[ series == "S3",], y="ke", 
             main = " Temperature vs. Total Energy")
```

We can look at a few runs (@fig-xn30 and @fig-xn100 below).

```{r}
#| label: fig-xn30
#| fig-cap: "`S3.0030` plot with first 1,000 steps skipped."
xn30 <- head( combineruns( datadir, "S3", "0030")$rundt, 
              MD2DF.D[ run == "S3.0030", total.steps])
plotMD2( as.data.frame( tail( xn30, -1000)), dt=0.01)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-xn100
#| fig-cap: "`S3.0100` with first 1,000 steps skipped."
xn100 <- head( combineruns( datadir, "S3", "0100", verbose=TRUE)$rundt,
               MD2DF.D[ run == "S3.0100", total.steps])
plotMD2( as.data.frame( tail( xn100, -1000)), dt=0.01)
```

So the previously observed steps are gone. We will import the data into
a new data table. There are 14 runs which are considered "not valid."

```{r}
#| label: rmxn100
# clean up
rm( xn30, xn100)
gc()
```

Next, we look at the variance of the total energy by run in
@fig-S2S3TEsd . The reduced deviation in the S3 runs shows that
excluding the potential energy step worked.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S2S3TEsd
#| fig-cap: The standard deviation of the total energy plotted by series. The S2 and S2b series did _not_ correct for the potential energy step, and as particles moved in and out of the range, so total energy would be afffected. (Vertical scale is logrithmic.)
ser <- as.factor( MD2DF.D$series)
lev <- levels( ser)
plot( TE.sd.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data = MD2DF.D, col = ser,
      log='y', pch = 19, xlab = "Mean Total Energy", ylab = "SD", 
      main = "Standard Deviation of Total Energy by Series")
 grid()
 legend( x = "bottomright", legend = lev, pch=19, col = 1:3)
```

Looking into the transition region (@fig-keTE.Dz) we can see the
distribution of samples in and around the transition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-keTE.Dz
#| fig-cap: Zoom into Series 3 data @fig-keTE.D
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.D[ series == "S3" & TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.14,0.155),],
             y="ke")
grid(col="darkgray")
```

We need more samples in the transition region (0.144 to 0.152), and the
randomness of the initialization energy will help with that.

```{r}
#| label: fig-delta-te
#| fig-cap: "Total energy change at each energy step. There is a fair amount of uncertainty starting in the transition region."
setkey( MD2DF.D, TE.mean.rs)
tt <- MD2DF.D[ series == "S3",]
plot( x = tail( tt$TE.mean.rs, -1), y=diff( tt$TE.mean.rs), 
      panel.first = grid(),
      xlab = "TE", ylab = expression(Delta * E), 
      main = "Energy Increment between Runs")
```

We also need more executions for the runs not yet declared valid, and
we'll include those in the transition regions too (@tbl-MD2DF.Dtrn)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-MD2DF.Dtrn
#| tbl-cap: Key values for transition region points in `MD2DF.D`.
knitr::kable( MD2DF.D[ series == "S3" & 
                       (TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.144, 0.152) | !valid), 
         .(energy, TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, ke.sd.rs, valid)])
```

That's nine energies: 29 through 37 (we need to both re-run and extend
these), plus eight more: 43, 46, 54, 64, 66, 81, 90, & 99. We already
know that we want to run 4M steps in the transition region, and we'll
add 60k steps to the remaining *not valid* runs.

## Second Tranche

Below is the record of the the additional executions.

``` julia
julia> tlist2 = [i for i in 29:37]

julia> @time MD2.newruns( td, tlist2, "S3b.", 10000, 10000, 400)

1572.568106 seconds (2.16 G allocations: 148.349 GiB, 3.00% gc time, 197 lock conflicts)

julia> tstr2 = [@sprintf("S3.%.4d", i) for i in tlist2]
julia> @time MD2.filerun_thread( td, tstr2, 7, 10000, 370)
1508.708704 seconds (1.99 G allocations: 136.938 GiB, 3.02% gc time, 141 lock conflicts, 0.12% compilation time)

julia> tlist3 = [43, 46, 54, 64, 66, 81, 90,  99]
julia> tstr3 = [@sprintf("S3.%.4d", i) for i in tlist3]
julia> @time MD2.filerun_thread( td, tstr3, 7, 10000, 6)
 24.146227 seconds (28.71 M allocations: 1.973 GiB, 3.13% gc time, 23 lock conflicts)
```

In the first statement (`newruns()`) I was not working at the computer,
and had shut the memory hog *Chrome*. That is nine runs of 401 10k-step
executions for 36,090k total steps which took 26m 12.54s (0.0436s/1k
steps). This is a bit slower, and is likely because *Julia* was started
with `julia --threads 7,1`, that's seven threads with one reserved for
garbage collection. Unsure exactly what this means, but only runs of
different energies can be run in parallel. I think that of the nine, six
run in parallel, and then three more. The extended runs in
`filerun_thread()` were executed while I was using *Chrome*, and were
nine runs of 370 10k-step executions for 33,300 total steps, which took
25m 8.7s (0.0453s/1k steps; and that was an error: it should have been
397 executions, not 370, so we are short of 4M steps by 269k steps). The
last run was eight runs of six 10k executions, for 480k steps for
0.0503s/1k steps. This next statement will create `MD2DF.E`:

```{r}
#| label: MD2DF.E
system.time( MD2DF.E <- MD2DFfile( "../MD2DF.E.RDS", datadir, "S3*.scalars.csv",
                                   df=MD2DF.D))
```

Did not get very parallel execution there. It may have been memory
issues, as I closed *Chrome*, *VSCode*, *Julia*, and an instance of
*RStudio* and I saw a few more cores used. That took almost 14 m. The
data is summarized in @fig-MD2DF.E below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.E
#| fig-cap: All (or most) of the 60 columns represented one way or another. The first nine plots are simply `plotScalars`. These are followed by (left to right, top to bottom) `TE Range` (`TE.max.raw - TE.min.raw` in open symbols, and `TE.sd.rs` in closed symbols, plotted logrithmically), Momentum squared (with standard deviation and range), Maximum of momentum squared vs. total steps, spectral width (in units of $1 / \tau$), $ \psi$ delta -  the difference berween `psiabs` and `psiavg`, and at the bottem left total steps.
op <- par( mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 0.5, 0.5), tcl = -0.3,
mgp = c(1.7, 0.4, 0))
plotAllMD2( MD2DF.E[ series == "S3" | series == "S3b"], linethresh = 200)
```

@fig-MD2DF.EkeTE show the temperature vs. energy plot of the new data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.EkeTE
#| fig-cap: Full series 3 plot of temperature (ke) vs total energy.
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.E[ series == "S3" | series=="S3b",], y="ke")
```

@fig-MD2DF.EkeTEz shows that are still a number of points not considered
valid, and a dearth of points in the transition region. The new points
overlapped the first set, so we may have to create some by hand, as the
run scripts take integers for the init temperature. We will also heat
some runs, but that is a separate investigation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.EkeTEz
#| fig-cap: Zoom into transition region of @fig-MD2DF.EkeTE
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.E[ (series == "S3" | series == "S3b") & 
                      TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.14,0.155),], y="ke")
grid(col="darkgray")
```

There are still eight runs not considered valid, but only three are well
outside the transition region (@tbl-MD2DF.Envalid).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-MD2DF.Envalid
#| tbl-cap: "*Not valid* runs in `MD2DF.E`."
setkey( MD2DF.E, TE.mean.rs)
knitr::kable( MD2DF.E[ series == "S3" | 
                       series == "S3b",][ valid==0,                                                           .(total.steps, TE.mean.rs, run)])
```

`S3.0081` is alone among the hot runs that are not considered valid.
@fig-xn81.E is a plot of that run.

```{r}
#| label: fig-xn81.E
#| fig-cap: Raw plots of `S3.0081` with first 1,000 steps skipped. Note the `combineruns()` function will combine all executions, not just the 91k steps which created the data point in `MD2DF.E`.  Only the `head()` of the data is used here.
xn81.E <- head( combineruns( datadir, "S3", "0081", verbose=TRUE)$rundt,
                MD2DF.E[ run == "S3.0081", total.steps])
plotMD2( as.data.frame( tail( xn81.E, -1000)), dt=0.01)
```

It's hard to see issues there. In figure @fig-xn81.Ekers the resampled
data perhaps shows a growing variance:

```{r}
#| label: fig-xn81.Ekers
#| fig-cap: "Run `S3.0081` kinetic energy resampled by 500 steps."
plot( rsmpavg( xn81.E$ke, 500), ylab="ke", panel.first=grid())
```

We'll round out the runs, doubling the 91k steps and reaching 4M for
those in the transition region.

``` julia
julia> tstr4 = ["S3.0046", "S3.0054", "S3.0081"]
julia> @time MD2.filerun_thread( td, tstr4, 13, 10000, 9)
 22.626391 seconds (32.58 M allocations: 1.915 GiB, 3.25% gc time, 22 lock conflicts, 124.21% compilation time: 3% of which was recompilation)
 
julia> @time MD2.filerun_thread( td, ["S3.0030", "S3.0032"], 377, 10000, 27)
 43.005529 seconds (32.29 M allocations: 2.220 GiB, 1.12% gc time, 7 lock conflicts)
```

These new executions will be incorporated into `MD2DF.F`, and the
updated transition region plotted in @fig-MD2DF.Ftr.

```{r}

MD2DF.F <- MD2DFfile( "../MD2DF.F.RDS", datadir, "S3*.scalars.csv", df=MD2DF.E)
setkey( MD2DF.F, TE.mean.rs)
```

```{r}

plotconfMD2( MD2DF.F[ (series == "S3" | series == "S3b") & 
                      TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.14,0.155),], y="ke")
```

```{r}

```

`S3.0081` still isn't there (@fig-xn81.F).

Process the data in `MD2DF.H`.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DF.H
MD2DF.H <- MD2DFfile( "../MD2DF.H.RDS", datadir, "S3*.scalars.csv", df=MD2DF.G)
setkey( MD2DF.H, TE.mean.rs)
```

And plot the transition region in @fig-MD2DF.HkeTEz.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.HkeTEz
#| fig-cap: Transition region zoom into `MD2DF.H`.
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.H[ (series == "S3" | series == "S3b") & 
                      TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.138,0.155),], y="ke")
grid(col="darkgray")
```

That's a surprise. The new point `S3.00275` temperature is below that of
the next higher energy (and also the next lower energy). This calls into
question the start of the transition region.

```{r}

#| tbl-cap: Key values for transition region points in `MD2DF.H`. 
knitr::kable( MD2DF.H[ series == "S3" | 
                       series == "S3b",][ valid==0 | TE.mean.rs %within% 
                                             c( 0.140, 0.145),
                  .(total.steps, steps.avg, TE.mean.rs, valid, run)])
```

The new data calls into question whether `S3.0027`, `S3.0028` or even
`S3.0026` are truly in equilibrium. All three of these need to be run to
to 4M steps (i.e., an additional 397 10k runs). The gap between
`S3.0026` and `S3.0027` is also a bit large: 0.00127 (see
@fig-delta-te), so we ought to fill that gap in with a 4M step run.

Let's see if we can tell what is going on with `S3.00275`:

```{r}

               MD2DF.H[ run == "S3.00275", total.steps])
plot( rsmpavg( xn275.H$ke, 500), ylab="ke", panel.first=grid())
```

@fig-xn275.H shows that the system is going in and out of melting.

```{r}

```

Lastly we'll look at the state of the Nelson-Halperin order parameter in

```{r}
#| label: fig-MD2DF.Hpsi
#| fig-cap: The magnitude of the complex Nelson-Halperin order parameter averaged over all steps (solid symbols), and the mean of the magnitude avereaged over 500 steps (open symbols). Blue circles considred valid, and red triangles not considered valid.
with( MD2DF.H[ series == "S3" | series == "S3b",] ,{
   pch <- rep_len( 16, length.out = length( valid)) # solid symbols
   pch[ valid == 0] <- 17
   col = rep_len( "darkblue", length.out = length( valid))
   col[ valid == 0] <- 'darkred'
   plot( x = TE.mean.rs, y = 1000 * psiavg, col = col, pch = pch,
   xlab = "Total Energy", ylab = expression(1000 * psi), log="y",
   panel.first = grid())
   pch <- pch - 15 # This will switch to open symbols
   points( x = TE.mean.rs, y = 1000 * psiabs.mean.rs, col = col, pch = pch)})
```

# Transition Region

The following is a closer look at the transition region. @tbl-MD2DF.Itr
lists key points in that region

```{r}
#| label: tbl-MD2DF.Itr
#| tbl-cap: "Key transition values (total energy between 0.140 and 0.148).  The `msd` values are the measured ke standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of samples, that is, it is the standard deviation of the mean ke."
knitr::kable( MD2DF.I[ series == "S3" | series == "S3b",][ valid==0 | TE.mean.rs %within% c( 0.140, 0.148),.(total.steps, steps.avg, TE.mean.rs, valid, run, ke.mean.rs, msd=ke.sd.rs/sqrt(nr))])
```

Now we have two 4M step runs labeled "valid" before the transition
region, and all runs not declared valid have around 4M points (with the
exception of the oddball `S3.0081`). We'll call `S3.0265` at 0.14231 the
top of the solid region. The bottom of the fluid region is not so clear,
as the 4M step run `S3b.0033` was not "valid" at at TE of 0.14872, but
it looks like it sits on the line, and there are three valid runs at
lower energies. We will choose `S3.0031` at TE of 0.14692 as the first
fully fluid run, although arguments could be made to go as low as
`S3b.0030` or even `S3b.00305`. The following code will generate
regressions of the solid and fluid regions (@fig-treg5).

```{r}
#| label: fig-treg5
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Unweighted regressions of kinetic and total energy."

minpe <- 0.127373 - 0.0114238 # Theoretical minimum PE
S3DT <- MD2DF.I[ series == "S3" | series == "S3b"]
temin <- 0.14232 # transition energy ,in, just above S3.00265
temax <- 0.14691 # transition region max, just below S3.0031
maxte <- max( S3DT$TE.mean.rs)
vs <- S3DT[ TE.mean.rs <= temin, .(run, ke.mean.rs, TE.mean.rs, ke.sd.rs, nr)]
setkey(vs, TE.mean.rs) # solid table
slm <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ I(TE.mean.rs - minpe) - 1, data=vs) # Solid lm with minpe
summary(slm)
slinex <- c(minpe, temin) # TE endpoints for solid line.
sliney <- predict( slm, data.frame( TE.mean.rs = slinex)) # solid line ke's
vf <- S3DT[ TE.mean.rs > temax, .(run, ke.mean.rs, TE.mean.rs, ke.sd.rs, nr, 
                                  ke.min.raw, ke.max.raw, valid, Fval)]
# ALL points above 0.157
setkey(vf, TE.mean.rs)
flm <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data=vf) # fluid lm of all points.
summary( flm)
cflm  <- coef( flm) # coefficients of fluid lm of all points.
tlinex <- c( temin, (sliney[2] - cflm[1]) / cflm[ 2])
# the right endpoint needs to be updated.
flinex <- c( tlinex[2], maxte)
fliney <- predict( flm, data.frame( TE.mean.rs = flinex))
tliney <- c( sliney[2],  sliney[2]) # trans. line y endpoints
plotconfMD2( y="ke", df = S3DT, 
             linethresh = 200, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle", 
             ylab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle") # sets up plot
grid( col = "darkgray") # replot grid so it sits in foreground of range area
lines( slinex, sliney, lwd = 2) # Solid line
lines( tlinex, tliney, lwd = 2, col = 'red') # transition line
lines( flinex, fliney, lwd = 2) # fluid line All pnts
pred.s.plim <- predict( slm, interval = "prediction") # solid prediction
matlines(vs$TE.mean.rs, pred.s.plim[,-1], lty = c(1,1), lwd = c(1,1), 
        col = c('blue','blue'), type = "l")
pred.f.plim <- predict( flm, interval = "prediction")
matlines(vf$TE.mean.rs, pred.f.plim[,-1], lty = c(1,1), lwd = c(1,1), 
        col = c('blue','blue'), type = "l")
text( x = tlinex, y = tliney, labels = format( tlinex, trim=TRUE, digits=4), 
      pos = c( 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
rpl <- recordPlot()
png("treg5.png", width = 600, height = 300)
replayPlot(rpl)
dev.off()
```

Those are very good fits, but zooming in (@fig-treg5z) shows there is
something else going on.

```{r}
#| label: fig-treg5z
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: 'Close‑up of the transition region from @fig-treg5, clearly showing where adding energy does not change the temperature. Thick black lines are regressions of the solid region (valid points below 0.14232), and the fluid region (all points above 0.14691), and the red line is the transition region drawn between (intersecting) the two regression lines. 1$\sigma$ confidence intervals of measurements are plotted as light blue region along with the regression lines, as well as gray region showing the maximum ‑ minimum range for each measurement. Points are shown as black circles and red triangles (valid and not valid points, respectively). 95% confidence intervals on the regression predictions are shown as thin blue lines.'

lines( slinex, sliney, lwd = 2) # Solid line
lines( tlinex, tliney, lwd = 2, col = 'red') # transition line

pred.s.plim <- predict( slm, interval = "prediction") # solid prediction

matlines(vf$TE.mean.rs, pred.f.plim[,-1], lty = c(1,1), lwd = c(1,1),
```

## Weighted Regression

The fluid line near the transition region systematically misses most of
the points. Perhaps a weighted regression will help. @fig-kesd looks at
the variances of the kinetic energy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kesd
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: 'Standard deviation of the resampled kinetic energy estimates as a function of the mean total energy.'

plot(ke.sd.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data = S3DT, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle",
ylab = "Estimated Std. Dev of KE mean")
grid()
```

That actually looks pretty linear. Let's see if it is.

```{r}
#| label: tesdlm

tesdlm <- lm( ke.sd.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data = S3DT[ !(TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.14, 0.16)),])
summary( tesdlm)
```

Let's see if setting the intercept at minimum TE to zero improves the
regression.

```{r}
#| label: tesdlm2

tesdlm2 <- lm( ke.sd.rs ~ I(TE.mean.rs - minpe) - 1, data = S3DT[ !(TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.14, 0.16)),])
summary( tesdlm2)
```

The higher regression coefficient is misleading, as it is calculated
differently for a slope-only regression. We need to develop a
theoretical foundation for this, but for the moment we'll simply reuse
the total energy regression as weight in the ke vs. TE regression.
First, we imposed an intercept by subtracting the minimum pe from the TE
in the regression. The *actual* intercept (zero TE on the graph) is
$-m E_{\text{minpe}}$, where $,m$ is the slope, and $E_{\text{minpe}}$
is the min pe. @fig-kesdreg shows the predicted points on that line.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kesdreg
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Standard deviation of the resampled kinetic energy estimates as a function of the mean total energy with simple slope-only regression line.  The dark green small points are the predicted standard deviations at each run's TE."

plotconf( y = S3DT$ke.sd.rs, x = S3DT$TE.mean.rs, Fval = S3DT$Fval, 
          xlab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle", 
          ylab = "Estimated Std. Dev of KE mean")
ctesdlm2 <- coef(tesdlm2)
abline( -minpe * ctesdlm2, ctesdlm2)

points( S3DT$TE.mean.rs, predict( tesdlm2, new = S3DT[,.(TE.mean.rs)]), 
        pch = 20, col = 'darkgreen')
grid()
```

The predictions above are the predicted standard deviation of the
re-sampled ke points. The mean ke is the average of those points, so the
variance of that average is the variance of the original data divided by
the number of samples in the average (@fig-tregz6).

```{r}
#| label: fig-tregz6
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Close‑up of the transition region as identified with weighted regression. As before, thick black lines are weighted regressions of the solid region (points with TE below 0.14232), and the fluid region (points above 0.14691), and the red line is the transition region drawn between (intersecting) the two regression lines. 1$\\sigma$ confidence intervals of measurements are plotted as light blue region along with the regression lines, as well as gray region showing the maximum ‑ minimum range for each measurement. Points are shown as black circles and red triangles (valid and not valid points, respectively). 95% confidence intervals on the regression predictions are shown in thin blue lines, and reflect the application of the weights (the confidence region is narrow where there are many samples)."

fw <- vf$nr / (predict( tesdlm2,  new = vf[,.(TE.mean.rs)])^2) # fluid weights
fwlm <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data=vf, weights = fw) # fluid lm
summary( fwlm)
cfwlm  <- coef( fwlm) # coefficients of fluid lm of all points.
tlinex2 <- c( temin, (sliney[2] - cfwlm[1]) / cfwlm[ 2])
flinex2 <- c( tlinex2[2], maxte)
fliney2 <- predict( fwlm, data.frame( TE.mean.rs = flinex2))
plotconfMD2( y="ke", df = S3DT[ TE.mean.rs %within% c( 0.135, 0.155),], 
             linethresh = 200, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle", 
             ylab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle") # sets up plot
grid( col = "darkgray") # replot grid so it sits in foreground of range area
lines( slinex, sliney, lwd = 2) # Solid line
lines( tlinex2, tliney, lwd = 2, col = 'red') # transition line
lines( flinex2, fliney2, lwd = 2) # fluid line All pnts
pred.s.plim <- predict( slm, interval = "prediction") # solid prediction
matlines(vs$TE.mean.rs, pred.s.plim[,-1], lty = c(1,1), lwd = c(1,1), 
        col = c('blue','blue'), type = "l")
pred.fw.plim <- predict( fwlm, interval = "prediction")
matlines(vf$TE.mean.rs, pred.fw.plim[,-1], lty = c(1,1), lwd = c(1,1), 
        col = c('blue','blue'), type = "l")
text( x = tlinex2, y = tliney, labels = format( tlinex2, trim=TRUE, digits=4), 
      pos = c( 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
rpl <- recordPlot()
png("tregz6.png", width = 600, height = 300)
replayPlot(rpl)
dev.off()
```

## Polynomial Regression

The classic way to do a polynomial regression is to increase the degree
until the AIC increases. This took some experimentation to accomplish
the results in @tbl-polyreg.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-polyreg
#| tbl-cap: AIC of poly fits from 2 though 8 degrees.
fplm <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 2), data=vf) # fluid lm
fwplm <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 2), data=vf, weights = fw) 
fwplm2 <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 3), data=vf, weights = fw) 
fwplm3 <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 5), data=vf, weights = fw) 
fwplm4 <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 6), data=vf, weights = fw) 
fwplm5 <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 7), data=vf, weights = fw) 
fwplm6 <- lm( ke.mean.rs ~ poly( TE.mean.rs, 8), data=vf, weights = fw)
knitr::kable( AIC( flm, fwlm, fplm, fwplm, fwplm2, fwplm3, fwplm4, fwplm5, fwplm6))
```

The best weighted fit is a seventh degree polynomial, which is, of
course, ridiculous. If we look at the significance of the coefficients
though, we see that the third order coefficient is the only one with any
real significance (until the 7th.)

```{r}
summary( fwplm5)
```

So the third order is possibly justified. Note also the second order
un-weighted regression has a similar AIC to the third order weighted.
The great disparity in the weights may be driving the fit in unjustified
ways. @fig-tregp is a plot of two polynomial fits.

The two lines substantially overlap with the data and each other, and so are difficult to distinguish. The blue lines are the confidence interval of the weighted fit.'

```{r}
summary( fplm)
summary( fwplm2)

plotconfMD2( y="ke", df = vf,  # just plot fluid region
             linethresh = 200, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle", 
             ylab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle") # sets up plot
grid( col = "darkgray") # replot grid so it sits in foreground of range area

lines( vf$TE.mean.rs, predict( fwplm2), lwd = 2) # fluid line All pnts
lines( vf$TE.mean.rs, predict( fplm), lwd = 2, col = "darkred", lty = 2) 
pred.fwp.plim <- predict( fwplm2, interval = "prediction")

        col = c('blue','blue'), type = "l")
```

# Specific Heat

The specific heat is the slope of the energy vs. temperature curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-EvT
#| fig-cap: "The total energy vs. temperature.  The dotted line is attempting to show the very small standard deviation of the energy points.  The red triangles are points not considered validly inequilibrium. Remember that the temperature data has significant standard deviations, but these are not displayed."
setkey( S3DT, ke.mean.rs)
plotconfMD2( x='ke.mean.rs', y="TE", df=S3DT[ TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.135,0.155)],
             linethresh=200, xlab="Kinetic Energy per Particle", 
             ylab ="Total Energy per Particle")# sets up plot
```

We need a numerical derivative function in order to compute
$C_v = dE / dT$. We will simply fit (really, *draw*) a line or curve
between a number of points, and compute the derivative of that line or
curve. `lm( y ~ poly( x, n), ...)` will fit a polynomial of degree `n`
to the values passed it, and if we pass `n + 1` values, the fit will be
exact (i.e., pass through the supplied points). The derivative will be
evaulated at the midpoint between the first and last point.

```{r}
#| label: dydx

dydx <- function( y, x, lag = 1) {
   # find derivative over lag + 1 points
   lx <- length( x)
   stopifnot( length( y) == lx)
   data <- data.table( x = x, y = y, keyby = x)
   xm <- (data$x[ 1:(lx - lag)] + data$x[ (lag + 1):lx]) / 2 # midpoint of eval sets
   dydxfit <- function( i) { # get dy/dx from points i:(i + lag)
      c <- coef( lm( y ~ poly( x, lag, raw = TRUE), # get poly coef
                     data = data[ i:(i + lag)]))
      dpc <- (1:lag) * tail( c, -1) # derivative of poly coeff
      polyval( rev(dpc), xm[ i]) # evaluate polynomial at midpoint of data & return
   }
   dd <- vapply( 1:(lx - lag), dydxfit, 1.0)
   list( dd=dd, xm = xm)
}

# test
tx <- c(1, 4, 3, 3.5, 2, 5)
ty <- tx^2
(dd <- dydx(ty, tx, 2)) # Note the NaN in third position: 3,  5, NaN, 7, 9
dd$dd - 2 * dd$xm
rm( tx, ty, dd) # remove these variables
```

A few different lags are plotted in @fig-Cv1.

The negative values are unrealistic, but not unsurprising due to the
fluctuations in the transition region. While the line looks pretty flat,
it also looks like it is zero, which is clearly a scaling issue: the
large values returned by the first difference causes the variations in
the rest of the line to be unnoticeable. We can also exclude the points

# Diffusion Estimates

## Making the Runs

We must select runs on which to estimate the diffusion. We will not use
all runs, but will do three solid, four fluid, and all in and near the
transition region. We will divide up the two regions into four and five
divisions, respectively. `S3.0001` at `TE = 0.11695` is the lowest
energy run, and `S3.0100` at `TE = 0.21554` is the highest.

```{r}
minte <- vs[ run == 'S3.0001', TE.mean.rs]
sde <- (temin - minte)/4 # solid delta energy
minte + sde * c(1, 2)
```

Runs `S3.0007` and `S3.0014` are the closest to those energies. All of
the \~4M step runs will have diffusion estimated (`S3.0026` through
`S3.0037`, including all of the `S3b.` runs), the highest energy one
being `S3.0037` at `TE = 0.15289`.

```{r}
fde <- (maxte - 0.15289)/5
0.15289 + fde * c( 1, 2, 3)
```

Runs `S3.0050`, `S3.0062`, and `S3.0075` are the runs closest to those
energies. The expression below will create a list (that can be copied
and pasted into *Julia* with some effort).

```{r}
#| eval: false
(drn <- c('S3.0001', 'S3.0007', 'S3.0014', S3DT[ total.steps > 100000, run], 
          'S3.0050', 'S3.0062', 'S3.0075', 'S3.0100')) # diffusion runs
```

## Reading in diffusion data

We can find all of the diffusion files via the following expressions and
function. (Note that when initially run, there all diffusion files did
not exist. Re-running this script however will find all diffusion files
in existence, and so will show updated results.)

```{r}
#| label: ddb
#| warning: false
# warnings are generated because the columns of the diff files have no names.

(diff_files <- list.files( datadir, glob2rx( "*.diff.*")))

read_diff <- function( datadir, runname) { # returns a data.table with diffusion data
   filename <- list.files( datadir, runname,full.names = TRUE)
   #print( filename)
   dd <- data.table::fread( filename)
   nrdd <- nrow( dd)
   ddcols <- colnames( dd)
   timecols <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=4, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dscols   <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=5, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dmxcols  <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=6, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dd[, row := 1:nrdd] # adds row number to show time sequence of executions
   dd[, run := rep( runname, nrdd)] # put run name in each row.
   reshape( dd, list( timecols, dscols, dmxcols),
            v.names=c("Time", "D2", "Dmax"), timevar="group", idvar="row", 
            drop=c("time","d^2", "max d^2"), direction="long")
}

# call on each element of diff_files, and bind into big data table
ddb <- rbindlist( lapply( diff_files, function(fn) read_diff( datadir, fn)))
head(ddb)
```

To get the mean displacement we must average by time and run. We will
soon need to correlate the run with those in the main MD2 data table, so
we need to drop the last nine characters of the file name.

```{r}
#| label: diffdata
diffdata <- ddb[, .(d2mn = mean( D2), d2sd = sd( D2), maxD = max( Dmax)), 
                by=.( Time, run)]
# next line uses a regex to replace last 9 characters with nothing/
diffdata$run <- gsub( '.{9}$', "", diffdata$run)
head( diffdata, n=20)
```

## Analysis of Max Motion

If the particles move near half the side distances, then the calculation
may be in error. What is recorded is $r^2$, and the maximum of that
quantity observed. Just as a reminder, our 256 particle system at a
density of $1 / \pi$ has the system size given by
$B_x = \frac{8 \sqrt{2 \pi}}{3^{1/4}}$ and $B_y = B_x\sqrt{3} / 2$ (so
$B_x =$ `r 8 * sqrt( 2 * pi)/3^(1/4)` and $B_y =$
`r (sqrt(3) / 2) * 8 * sqrt( 2 * pi)/3^(1/4)`). We can find the overall
max observed and its source via the following:

```{r}
sqrt( mxd2 <- max( diffdata$maxD))
diffdata[ which.max( diffdata$maxD == mxd2),]
```

That is a bigger than $B_y/2$
(`r (sqrt(3) / 4) * 8 * sqrt( 2 * pi)/3^(1/4)`), although the vector is
likely not aligned with either of the dimensions. @fig-allD2 shows all
of the diffusion measurements on one graph.

```{r}
#| label: fig-allD2
#| fig-cap: "All $r^2$ measurements from all runs.  Each of the 36 runs is given one of 6 'open' symbols (so the symbols are re-used). the red dashed line is $B_y/2$."
plot( sqrt(maxD) ~ Time, data=diffdata, xlim = c(0, 50), 
      pch = mod( as.integer( as.factor( diffdata$run)), 6))
abline( h = (sqrt(3) / 4) * 8 * sqrt( 2 * pi)/3^(1/4), lty=2, col = 'darkred')
```

This begs for improvements to the diffusion measurement apparatus.

## Diffusion Estimates

Now we need to perform a linear regression on the data, and we need to
determine if there really is no trend, if there is a linear trend, or if
there is a curve to the trend. To do this, we'll do a linear regression
with an intercept, a regression without an intercept (if there is
diffusion, $D(t) = 0$), and a second degree polynomial regression. For
each regression, we'll record the coefficients, the regression
coefficient, and the f-value.

First though, let's look at some of the data. @fig-exdifplt plots four
diffusion lines.

```{r}
#| label: fig-exdifplt
#| fig-cap: Mean estimated diffusion for four progressivly hotter runs.  `S3.0001` is the coldest run, and `S3.0081` is the hottest.
wdd <- dcast( diffdata, Time ~ run, value.var = 'd2mn') # long-to-wide
pl <- c('S3.0001', 'S3.0031', 'S3.0046', 'S3.0081')
matplot( wdd$Time, wdd[, ..pl], pch=1:4, type="b", xlab = 'Time',
         ylab=expression(r^2), panel.first=grid(), xlim=c(0, 50), 
         main = 'Some Example Diffusion Plots')
legend( x="topleft", pl, pch=1:4, col=1:4)
```

We need a function to do a few fits for us, and plot the results.
Initially, I fit a line, a line without an intercept, a 2nd degree
polynomial, and `I(Time^2)` (parabola without intercept). None of these
were very helpful, and while the 2nd degree polynomial did appear to be
somewhat more significant on the hot runs, the 2nd degree polynomial was
*always* statistically significant, so the function below only fits the
line with intercept.

```{r}
#| label: fitdiff
fitdiff <- function( r, diffdata, plot=FALSE, verbose = FALSE) { 
   # include the run ID in r as a string
   dd <- diffdata[ r == run,]
   # print( nrow(dd))
   maxT <- max( dd$Time)
   maxd <- max( dd$d2mn)
   
   #lm0 <- lm( d2mn ~ Time - 1, data = dd)
   lm1 <- lm( d2mn ~ Time, data = dd)
   #lm2 <- lm( d2mn ~ poly( Time, 2), data = dd)
 
   if (plot) {
      newT <- data.frame( Time =c( 0, dd$Time)) # Predict value at Time = 0
      pred.w.plim <- predict( lm1, newT, interval = "prediction")
      pred.w.clim <- predict( lm1, newT, interval = "confidence")
      plot( d2mn ~ Time, data = dd, xlim = c( 0, maxT), ylim = c(0, maxd), 
              main = r, xlab = 'Time', ylab = expression( r^2))
      grid()
      matplot(newT, cbind( pred.w.clim, pred.w.plim[, -1]), 
              col = c( 1, 2, 2, 3, 3), lty = c(1,2,2,3,3), type = "l", 
              add = TRUE)
      #abline( lm1)
      abline( h = mean( dd$d2mn), lty = 4, col = 4)
      legend( x = 'bottomright',  pch = c(1, NA, NA, NA, NA), 
              lty = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4), col = c( 1, 1, 2, 3, 4),
              legend = c("Measurements", 'Regression Line', "Conf. Interval",                            'Pred. Interval', 'Mean'))
   }
   if (verbose) {
      #print( summary( lm0))
      print( summary( lm1))
      #print( summary( lm2))
   }
   nr <- nrow( dd)
   mod <- summary( lm1)
   coeff <- unname( mod$coefficients[ "Time", c( 'Estimate', 'Std. Error')])
   t <- mod$fstatistic
   Fpvalue <-  stats::pf( t['value'], t['numdf'], t['dendf'], lower.tail=FALSE)
   data.table::data.table( run = r, nrd = nr, Estimated = coeff[1], 
      Std.Errord = coeff[2], r.squaredd = mod$r.squared, 
      Fvald =  unname( t['value']), Fpvalued = unname( Fpvalue), 
      dfd = t['dendf'])
}
```

Each temperature region has a particular character. Figures [-@fig-df01]
through [-@fig-df46] show a cold, hot and transition diffusion
estimates. The first is the coldest run and shows no diffusion.

```{r}
#| label: fig-df01
fitdiff( "S3.0001", diffdata = diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

The hot run shows a possible parabolic response.

```{r}
#| label: fig-df81
fitdiff( "S3.0081", diffdata = diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

The next two are around and above the transition region. Both show
highly linear response with intercepts near, but statistically
significant from, the origin.

```{r}
#| label: fig-df31
fitdiff( "S3.0031", diffdata = diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-df46
fitdiff( "S3.0046", diffdata = diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```

Lastly, we'll look at the way the standard deviation of the diffusion
estimates change over the length of time estimated in @fig-diffsd.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffsd
#| fig-cap: Standard deviation as a percent of the diffusion estimate plotted agains the time duration over which the diffuaion was estimated.
setkeyv( diffdata, c("run", "Time"))
plot(100 * d2sd / d2mn ~ Time, data = diffdata[ run %in% pl,], 
     pch = as.integer( factor( run)), col = as.integer( factor( run)), 
     ylab = "SD as %")
legend( x="topleft", legend = pl, col = 1: length(pl), pch = 1:length(pl))
grid()
```

This is good news. `S3.0031` is close to the transition region so it
might be expected to have a variance higher than the other runs. That
they are so tightly grouped fits the theory (the diffusion will be
proportional to temperature, and the variance is also proportional to
temperature).

I looked at multiple types of regression (with and without intercept,
second degree polynomial, and simple $T^2$ with no intercept, but *all*
worked pretty well always, so I stuck with simple linear regression
reporting the slope). `fitdiff()` will do this for us, with the
`diffdata` data table passed in as a second parameter in `lapply()`.

```{r}
#| label: S3DTdiff
difflist <- unique( diffdata$run)
diffproc <- data.table::rbindlist( lapply( difflist, fitdiff, diffdata))
S3DTdiff <- diffproc[ S3DTb, on = 'run']
```

The data table `S3DTdiff` now has the diffusion estimates (which is just
the slope of the regression line) added to the full data table.
@fig-treg8z shows the transition region with points at which diffusion
was measured highlighted.

```{r}
#| label: fig-treg8z
#| fig-cap: "@fig-treg7z with the points on which diffusion was estimated over-plotted with green triangles (which is pretty much all of them)."
plotconfMD2( y = "ke", df = S3DTb[ TE.mean.rs %within% c( 0.135, 0.155),], 
            linethresh = 200, xlab = "Total Energy per Particle", 
            ylab = "Kinetic Energy per Particle")# sets up plot
points( ke.mean.rs ~ TE.mean.rs, data = S3DTdiff[ !is.na( nrd),], pch = 0, 
        col = "green")
lines( tlinex2, tliney, lwd = 2, col = 'red') # transition line
text( x = tlinex2, y = tliney, labels = format( tlinex2, trim=TRUE, digits=4), 
      pos = c( 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
rpl <- recordPlot()
png("tregz8.png", width = 600, height = 300)
replayPlot(rpl)
dev.off()
```

@fig-fulldiffplot shows the measured diffusion.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fulldiffplot
#| fig-cap: THe measured diffusion as a function of temperature.
plot( Estimated ~ ke.mean.rs, data = S3DTdiff[ !is.na( nrd),], xlab = 'ke', 
      ylab = expression( r^2), main =  "Diffusion vs. Temperature")
grid()
```

@fig-diffplotz zooms into the jump, clearly showing that some points may
not be in equilibrium.

```{r}
grid()
```

The diffusion starts bouncing around, but we do not see a steady state
approaching the transition. We need more points. As of 7 May 2025, here

```{r}
                       .(run, valid, ke.mean.rs, TE.mean.rs, nrd)])
```

The following code will create the new record.

```{r}
#| label: diffdata2
#| warning: false
# warnings will be generated.
(diff_files2 <- paste( drn3, ".diff.txt", sep="")) # names of all diff files
ddb2 <- rbindlist( lapply( diff_files2, function(fn) read_diff( datadir, fn)))
# ddb2 has the full set of observations.
head(ddb2)
# diffdata2 holds the mean 
diffdata2 <- ddb2[, .(d2mn = mean(D2), d2sd = sd(D2), maxD = max(Dmax)), 
                  by = .( Time, run)]
# next line uses a regex to replace last 9 characters with nothing
diffdata2$run <- gsub( '.{9}$', "", diffdata2$run)
head( diffdata2, n=20)
difflist2 <- unique( diffdata2$run)
diffproc2 <- data.table::rbindlist( lapply( difflist2, fitdiff, diffdata2))
S3DTdiff2  <- S3DTdiff[ diffproc2, `:=`( 
      nrd = i.nrd, Estimated = i.Estimated, Std.Errord = i.Std.Errord, 
      r.squaredd = i.r.squaredd, Fvald = i.Fvald, Fpvalued = i.Fpvalued, 
      dfd = i.dfd), on="run"]
```

Finally, add the diffusion data to the `MD2DF` data table and save.

```{r}
MD2DF.L <- merge(MD2DF.K, S3DTdiff2[, .(run, nrd, Estimated, Std.Errord, 
      r.squaredd, Fvald, Fpvalued, dfd)], by = "run", all = TRUE)
saveRDS( MD2DF.L, file = "../MD2DF.L.RDS")
```

@fig-diffplot2z shows the complete diffusion data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffplot2z
#| fig-cap: "Updated diffusion plot, confidence intervals (the standard error of the estimate) shown in light blue."
setkey( S3DTdiff2, ke.mean.rs)
with( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd),], {
  plotconf( y = Estimated, x = ke.mean.rs, sd = Std.Errord, xlab = 'ke', 
      ylab = "4D", main =  "Diffusion vs. Temperature", Fval = Fval,
      xlim = c(0.012,0.014), ylim = c(0.0, 0.05))
})
grid()
```

We can compute numerical derivatives of this data. The four-point
derivative (lag = 3) fails (@fig-dDdTz).

```{r}
#| label: fig-dDdTz
#| fig-cap: "Zoom into the numerical derivative at three different lags. The lag 3 return `NA` for a number of points near the transition (a result of ill-conditioned regressions)."
#setkey(S3DT, TE.mean.rs)
with( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd),], {
   dDdT <- dydx( Estimated, ke.mean.rs)
   plot( x = dDdT$xm, y = dDdT$dd, panel.first = grid(), xlim=c(0.0120,0.0140),
         xlab="ke", ylab = "d(4D)/dT", typ = 'b', main = "d(4D)/dT, three lags.",
         ylim = c( -200, 200))
   dDdT2 <- dydx( Estimated, ke.mean.rs, lag = 2)
   points( x = dDdT2$xm, y = dDdT2$dd, typ = 'b', col='red')
   dDdT3 <- dydx( Estimated, ke.mean.rs, lag = 3)
   points( x = dDdT3$xm, y = dDdT3$dd, typ = 'b', col='green')
   legend( "topright", c("1", "2", "3"), pch=1, col=c('black','red','green'), 
           title = "Lag")
})
```

When the estimated $d r^2/ dT$ is below 0.01, the substance appears to
be more-or-less solid. Zooming into the transition region, we can see a
few poits that might appear to be starting to experience diffusion
(@fig-diffplot2z2). In particular, the last three points look like they
are increasing, and the standard error band excludes zero (meaning that
zero diffusion is outside one standard deviation of the estimate).

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffplot2z2
with( S3DTdiff2[ Estimated < 0.01,], {
  plotconf( y = Estimated, x = ke.mean.rs, sd = Std.Errord, xlab = 'ke', 
      ylab = "4D", main =  "Diffusion vs. Temperature", Fval = Fval,
      #xlim = c(0.0,0.013), ylim = c(0.0, 0.0012))
  )
})
abline( h = 0.0)
grid( col='darkgrey')
```

@tbl-S3DTdiff2tr lists points in transition region with small estimates
of $4D$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-S3DTdiff2tr
#| tbl-cap: "Diffusion estimates with temperature between 0.010 and 0.0135, and estimates of $4D$ (the `Estimated` column) between 0.0006 and 0.02."
knitr::kable( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd) & (ke.mean.rs %within% c(0.010, 0.0135) & (Estimated %within% c(0.0006, 0.02))), 
           .(run, ke.mean.rs, Estimated, Std.Errord, Fvald, Fpvalued) ])
```

So, it appears as though those last three points are not showing
diffusion, even though they are hotter than other points clearly showing
diffusion signs. Indeed, the P-value of the estimate shows that the
diffusion estimates are time-correlated with high probability. @fig-FpvD
shows the P-value of the regression against the estimated diffusion.

```{r}
#| label: fig-FpvD
#| fig-cap: "Log-log plot of F-Pvalue of the regression (log-scale) against the absolute value of estimated diffusion (small diffusion values are sometimes slightly negative).  The P-value of all estimates such that $4D > 0.01$ are very small, indicating that the regressions are highly statistically significant."
with( S3DTdiff2, {
  plotconf( y = Fpvalued, x = abs(Estimated), xlab = '|4D|', 
      ylab = "P(f)", main =  "P-Value of Regression vs. 4D", log='xy', 
      panel.first = grid( col='darkgrey'))
})

```

Let's look at `S3.0027` (@fig-df27). Definitely no diffusion happening
here.

```{r}
#| label: fig-df27
#| fig-cap: "Diffusion estimate for `S3.0027`."
fitdiff( "S3.0027", diffdata = diffdata, plot = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
```
